title: Making water safer in an emergency
h1: Making water safer in an emergency
dek: Boiling, filtering and disinfecting each solve some problems and miss others. What the CDC's current guidance covers, and the situations where nothing you can do at home is enough.
description: How to make questionable water safer to drink using the CDC's current guidance: boiling, bleach, tablets, filters and light, plus the cases where none of them works.
recheck: Immediately if the CDC revises either source below; otherwise at the next quarterly source sweep.

safety_review.scope: Approved as drafted, no changes requested. Includes the CDC/EPA altitude reconciliation (3 min near or above ~5,000 ft) and the EPA-only chlorine-odor check. Approval recorded from the reviewer's one-word reply in chat; item-by-item checklist notes were not supplied.

source_use.epa-emergency-disinfection: Independent check of boiling and bleach dosing; the 5,000-foot elevation threshold; bleach selection and age; the statement that boiling does not remove salts, heavy metals and most chemicals; the EPA Safe Drinking Water Hotline.
source_use.cdc-water-safe: Boiling times, bleach table for 5-9% sodium hypochlorite, tablets and drops, filter pore sizes, UV and solar disinfection, and the statement that fuel, toxic chemicals and radioactive material cannot be removed by boiling or disinfecting.
source_use.cdc-water-store: Bottled-water priority, how much to store, container cleaning and sanitizing steps, storage conditions, and replacement interval.
source_use.usscm-brenckle-2019: Naval water allowances in the 1802 regulations, the 1813 Constitution water load, and Captain Porter's cask rules (history panel only).
